problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.description:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth `0`.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Longest path is 3 -> 20 -> 15.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the widest level
hints: The depth of a tree is related to the depth of its subtrees.
depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)); an empty node has depth 0.
Recurse (or run a level-by-level BFS and count levels). Remember to build the tree from the array first.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.description:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, mirror it: swap the left and right child of every node. Return the root of the inverted tree.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`. Return the inverted tree in the same encoding, with trailing `null` values removed. An empty tree is `[]`.

examples.explanation: The only child moves from the left to the right.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Think about what happens to a single node and its two children.
Inverting a tree = swap the two children, then invert each child subtree.
Recurse (or use a queue). Serialize the result level by level, trimming trailing nulls.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.description:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return `true` if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).

In a valid BST, for every node all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's value, all values in its right subtree are strictly greater, and both subtrees are themselves valid BSTs. Duplicates therefore make a tree invalid.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: The node 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Checking only parent-child pairs is not enough. A node must respect every ancestor.
Pass down an allowed open interval (low, high) for each node; going left tightens high, going right tightens low.
Alternatively, an in-order traversal of a BST must be strictly increasing. Compare each visited value with the previous one.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
problems.description:
You are given a binary search tree (all values distinct) as a level-order array with `null` for missing children, plus two values `p` and `q` that both exist in the tree.

Return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` in its subtree (a node counts as a descendant of itself).

examples.explanation: A node can be an ancestor of the other.

constraints: `p != q` and both are present in the tree
problems.complexity: O(h) time, O(1) space
hints: Use the BST ordering: values on the left are smaller, on the right are larger.
Start at the root. If both p and q are smaller, the answer is in the left subtree; if both are larger, go right.
The first node where p and q fall on different sides (or equal the node) is the LCA. This is a simple loop.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.description:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the values of its nodes grouped by depth: a list of lists, where the first list holds the root, the second the root's children from left to right, and so on.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`. An empty tree gives `[]`.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: You need to visit nodes in an order that finishes one depth before starting the next.
Breadth-first search with a queue does exactly that.
At each step, snapshot the queue size k; the next k nodes form one level. Push their children for the next round.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.description:
A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each consecutive pair is connected by a parent-child edge, and no node appears twice. The path does not need to pass through the root and must contain at least one node.

The path sum is the sum of the node values along the path. Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum over all possible paths. Node values may be negative.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Path 15 -> 20 -> 7 skips the root.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: A best path has a highest node (its top). Think about what it looks like from that node's point of view.
For each node compute the best downward path starting at it: node.val + max(0, left gain, right gain). Negative gains are better dropped.
While computing gains, update a global answer with node.val + max(0, leftGain) + max(0, rightGain), which is the best path bending at this node. Use an iterative post-order or recursion.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.description:
Given the `root` of a binary search tree (distinct values) and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th smallest value in the tree, where `k = 1` means the smallest.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.
problems.complexity: O(h + k) time, O(h) space
hints: What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce?
In-order visits nodes in ascending order, so the k-th visited node is the answer.
Walk iteratively with a stack: go left as far as possible, pop and count, then move right. Stop at the k-th pop without visiting the rest.

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
problems.description:
Design a trie that supports three operations on lowercase strings:

- `insert(word)` stores a word.
- `search(word)` returns `true` only if that exact word was inserted earlier.
- `startsWith(prefix)` returns `true` if any inserted word begins with `prefix`.

To fit the function-call format, you receive a list `ops` of operations, each written as `[name, argument]` (for example `["insert", "apple"]`). Process them in order and return a list of results with one entry per operation: `null` for `insert`, and a boolean for `search` and `startsWith`.

examples.explanation: "app" is only a prefix until it is inserted itself.

constraints: Every argument is a non-empty string of 1 to 100 lowercase letters
problems.complexity: O(L) time per operation, O(total characters) space
hints: A hash set of words answers search, but what about prefixes?
Store words as paths of nodes: each node maps a letter to a child, and has a flag marking the end of a word.
insert walks/creates nodes along the word and sets the flag on the last one. search walks and checks the flag; startsWith walks and only checks the path exists.

problems.title: Word Search II
problems.description:
You are given an `m x n` grid of lowercase letters `board` and a list of distinct `words`. Return every word from the list that can be formed by a path through the grid.

A path moves between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, and the same cell may not be used twice within a single word. Words may be returned in any order, and each found word appears once in the output.

examples.explanation: Reaching the second b would reuse a cell.

constraints: Board and words use lowercase letters; all words are distinct
problems.complexity: O(m*n*4*3^(L-1)) time worst case, O(total word characters) space
hints: Running a separate Word Search for every word repeats a lot of work.
Put all words into a trie, then DFS from each cell, walking the trie in step with the board so dead prefixes are cut immediately.
Mark visited cells during the DFS and restore them. When you reach a trie node holding a word, record it and clear it so it is not reported twice; optionally prune exhausted trie branches.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th largest element in sorted order (not the k-th distinct value). Duplicates count separately: in `[5,5,4]` the 2nd largest is `5`.

Try to do better than sorting the whole array.
problems.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). You only care about the top k values.
Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far; its root is the current k-th largest.
For each number, push it; if the heap exceeds size k, pop the smallest. After one pass the root is the answer.

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.description:
Design a structure that receives integers one at a time and can report the median of everything received so far. The median is the middle value of the sorted numbers; with an even count it is the average of the two middle values.

To fit the function-call format you receive a list `ops` of operations: `["addNum", x]` adds a number and `["findMedian"]` queries the median. Return a list with one entry per operation: `null` for `addNum`, and the median (a number) for `findMedian`. Medians are always exact: whole values are returned as integers and halves as `x.5`. `findMedian` is only called after at least one `addNum`.
problems.complexity: O(log n) per addNum, O(1) per findMedian, O(n) space
hints: Re-sorting on every query is too slow. What do you need access to? Just the middle element(s).
Split the numbers into a lower half (max-heap) and an upper half (min-heap) so the middle values sit at the two roots.

Add to the lower half, move its max to the upper half, then if the upper half is larger move its min back. Keep sizes equal or lower = upper + 1. The median is the lower root, or the average of both roots.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.description:
A CPU must run a list of tasks, each labelled with a capital letter. One task takes one time unit, and the CPU may also sit idle for a unit. The same label may not run twice within `n` time units of each other: after running a task labelled `X`, at least `n` other units (tasks or idle) must pass before `X` runs again. Tasks can run in any order.

Return the minimum number of time units needed to finish all tasks.

examples.explanation: A B idle A B idle A B
No cooldown, so no idle time.

problems.complexity: O(t) time, O(1) space
hints: The most frequent task is the bottleneck. How must it be spread out?
If the top task appears f times, it creates f-1 gaps of length n between runs, giving a frame of (f-1)*(n+1) slots plus the final run.
Answer = max(len(tasks), (f-1)*(n+1) + k), where k is how many tasks tie for frequency f. Extra tasks fill idle gaps, and if gaps overflow, no idle time is needed at all.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.description:
You are given a 2D grid of the strings `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water). An island is a maximal group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically (diagonals do not connect). Everything outside the grid is water.

Return the number of islands.

examples.explanation: Diagonal neighbours are not connected.

problems.complexity: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space worst case
hints: Each island is a connected component. How could you count components in a grid?
Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, you have found a new island: count it, then flood-fill everything connected to it.
Flood fill with an explicit stack/queue (avoids deep recursion) and mark visited cells, e.g. by turning land into water in a copy.

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.description:
There are `numCourses` courses labelled `0` to `numCourses - 1`. The list `prerequisites` contains pairs `[a, b]`, meaning you must complete course `b` before you can take course `a`.

Return `true` if it is possible to finish all courses, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Each course requires the other first.

problems.complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
hints: Model courses as nodes and prerequisites as directed edges. When is it impossible?
It is impossible exactly when the graph has a cycle.
Run Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with in-degree 0 and reduce the in-degree of their dependents. If you process all courses, there is no cycle.

solutions.python:
from collections import deque


def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indeg = [0] * num_courses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return done == num_courses

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.description:
A network has `n` nodes labelled `1` to `n`. The list `times` holds directed links `[u, v, w]`: a signal sent from `u` reaches `v` after `w` time units.

A signal is sent from node `k`. Return the time it takes until every node has received it, or `-1` if some node can never be reached.

examples.explanation: Node 2 has no outgoing links, so node 1 is never reached.

constraints: Multiple links between the same pair of nodes are allowed
problems.complexity: O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space
hints: The signal travels along the fastest route to each node. What problem is that?
It is single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights, so Dijkstra's algorithm applies.
Run Dijkstra from k with a min-heap. The answer is the largest shortest distance, or -1 if any node stayed unreached.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.description:
An undirected graph on nodes `1..n` started as a tree (connected, no cycles) and then had exactly one extra edge added, so it now contains exactly one cycle. The graph is given as a list of `edges` in the order they were added.

Return the edge that, when removed, turns the graph back into a tree. If several edges lie on the cycle, return the one that appears **last** in `edges`.

examples.explanation: The cycle is 1-2-3-4; the last of those edges listed is [1,4].

constraints: No repeated edges and no self-loops
problems.complexity: O(n * alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
hints: Adding an edge between two nodes already connected creates a cycle.
Process edges in order and track connected groups with Union-Find.
The first edge whose endpoints already share a root closes the cycle; it is the last cycle edge in input order, so return it.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.description:
You are given two words `begin_word` and `end_word` of equal length, and a list of words `word_list`. A transformation sequence changes one letter at a time, and every word after the first must be in `word_list`.

Return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from `begin_word` to `end_word` (counting both ends), or `0` if no sequence exists. `begin_word` does not have to be in the list, but `end_word` must be.

examples.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog
end_word is not in the list.

constraints: All words are lowercase; words in the list are distinct
problems.complexity: O(N * L^2) time, O(N * L^2) space
hints: Treat words as nodes, with an edge between words that differ by one letter. The shortest sequence is a shortest path.
Breadth-first search finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
Avoid comparing all pairs: bucket words by wildcard patterns ("h*t", "*ot", "ho*"). Words sharing a pattern are neighbours. BFS level by level and count words.

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.description:
A foreign language uses the lowercase English letters, but in an unknown alphabetical order. You are given `words`, a list of words sorted lexicographically according to that unknown order.

Deduce an ordering of the letters that appears in `words` consistent with the list. Only letters that appear in the words are included in the answer. If several orderings are valid, return the lexicographically smallest one (compare as ordinary English strings). If the list is inconsistent (for example it contains a cycle of constraints, or a longer word appears before its own prefix), return the empty string `""`.

examples.explanation: z < x and x < z contradict each other.

problems.complexity: O(C + V log V) time where C is total characters and V <= 26
hints: Compare neighbouring words: the first position where they differ tells you one ordering rule between two letters.
Rules form a directed graph over the letters. A valid alphabet is a topological order; a cycle means no answer.
Beware the prefix case ("abc" before "ab" is impossible). Use Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap on available letters so ties resolve to the smallest letter, and fail if not every letter was placed.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.description:
You have coins of several denominations in `coins` and an `amount` of money. Each denomination can be used any number of times.

Return the fewest coins needed to make exactly `amount`, or `-1` if it cannot be made. An amount of `0` needs `0` coins.
problems.complexity: O(amount * coins) time, O(amount) space
hints: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails for sets like [1,3,4] and amount 6.
Let best[a] be the fewest coins for amount a. It depends on best[a - c] for each coin c.
best[0] = 0; best[a] = 1 + min(best[a - c]) over coins with c <= a, ignoring unreachable states. Answer best[amount], or -1 if it is still infinite.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements, and the chosen values must strictly increase.

examples.explanation: For example 2, 3, 7, 101.
Equal values are not strictly increasing.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: A simple DP: dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence ending at i. That is O(n^2).
To speed up, keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. tails is always sorted.
For each x, binary search the first tails entry >= x and replace it (or append if none). The final length of tails is the answer.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.description: Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of single-character operations needed to turn `word1` into `word2`. The allowed operations are: insert a character, delete a character, and replace a character.

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse -> rose -> ros

problems.complexity: O(m*n) time, O(n) space
hints: Compare the ends of the two strings. What can you do with the last characters?
Let d[i][j] be the distance between the first i chars of word1 and the first j of word2. If the characters match, d[i][j] = d[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).
Base cases: d[i][0] = i and d[0][j] = j. Each row only needs the previous one, so a rolling array suffices.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.description: Given a string `s` and a list of words `word_dict`, return `true` if `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more dictionary words (spaces inserted between them). A dictionary word may be reused any number of times.
problems.complexity: O(n * L) time with L the longest word, O(n) space
hints: Ask whether a prefix of s can be segmented, and build up from short prefixes.
ok[i] = true if the first i characters can be split. ok[0] = true.
ok[i] is true if some j < i has ok[j] true and s[j:i] in the dictionary. Only try j within the longest word length of i.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.description: Given an array of positive integers `nums`, return `true` if you can split it into two groups (every element in exactly one group) whose sums are equal, and `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: [1,5,5] and [11] both sum to 11.
The total, 11, is odd.

problems.complexity: O(n * sum) time, O(sum) space
hints: If the total is odd the answer is immediately false.
Otherwise you need a subset that sums to total/2. This is the subset-sum (0/1 knapsack) problem.
Let reach[s] be true if some subset sums to s. For each number x, update s from high to low: reach[s] |= reach[s - x]. Answer reach[total/2].

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.description:
There are `n` balloons in a row, the i-th holding the number `nums[i]`. You burst every balloon, one at a time. Bursting balloon `i` earns `left * nums[i] * right` coins, where `left` and `right` are the numbers on the balloons currently adjacent to it. If a neighbour does not exist (the edge of the row), treat its number as `1`.

Return the maximum total coins you can earn by choosing the best bursting order.
problems.complexity: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
hints: Thinking about which balloon to burst first makes neighbours change and subproblems interact.
Reverse the thinking: choose the LAST balloon to burst in a range. Then its neighbours are the range boundaries, so left and right parts become independent.
Pad nums with 1 on both ends. dp[i][j] = max over k in (i, j) of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j], filling by increasing gap. Answer dp[0][n+1].

problems.title: Regular Expression Matching
problems.description:
Implement matching of a string `s` against a pattern `p` that supports two special characters:

- `.` matches any single character.
- `*` matches zero or more copies of the character immediately before it (that character may itself be `.`).

The match must cover the entire string, not just part of it. Return `true` if `s` matches `p`.

examples.explanation: The pattern covers only one 'a'.
`.*` matches any run of characters.

constraints: p uses lowercase letters, `.` and `*`; every `*` follows a letter or `.`
problems.complexity: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
hints: Think of matching a suffix or prefix of s against a prefix or suffix of p; subproblems repeat.
Let dp[i][j] mean s[:i] matches p[:j]. If p[j-1] is a normal char or '.', it must match s[i-1] and dp[i-1][j-1] must hold.
If p[j-1] is '*', either use zero copies (dp[i][j-2]) or one more copy when the preceding pattern char matches s[i-1] (dp[i-1][j]). Fill dp[0][j] for patterns like a*b* matching the empty string.

problems.title: N-Queens (Count Solutions)
problems.description:
Place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two queens attack each other: no two may share a row, a column, or a diagonal.

Return the number of distinct valid placements. (Rotations and reflections count as different placements.)

examples.explanation: There are two valid boards.

problems.complexity: O(n!) time worst case, O(n) space
hints: Each row must contain exactly one queen, so decide a column row by row.
Track which columns and which two diagonal families are already used. Cells on the same diagonal share row-col, on the same anti-diagonal share row+col.
Backtrack: for each row try every free column, mark it (sets or bitmasks), recurse to the next row, and unmark. Count the times you place the last row.
